description:
We both are Techies. 
We are colaborating to make software for monitoring health of astronauts.
summary:
We built AstroHealth, an offline-first clinical decision support dashboard for astronauts and Crew Medical Officers, for use on ISS, Lunar Artemis and Mars transit missions. Earth telemedicine in real time is not possible due to 22 minutes of deep-space communication lag, so crews need independent medical triage that can operate without ground contact.

It’s a combination of absolute thresholds and acute red-flag symptom overrides, personalized space-baseline z-score drift, 3-day worsening trends and measurement cadence tracking. All rules and clinical protocols are bundled offline. Crews assess risk using an interactive 3D astronaut body map, record daily biometrics using side-by-side measurement guides, conduct PVT-Lite reaction tests and ONSD ultrasound caliper checks, follow Earth-independent Mars triage checklists, export medical report packets, and optionally query a protocol AI assistant.

AstroHealth supports autonomous crew care for Artemis and Mars and serves as a blueprint for remote clinics and disaster medicine on Earth, allowing for a zero connectivity approach to catching subtle spaceflight health drift early.
Github Link:(https://github.com/Deadpoets888/astro-health-monitor)
details:
What does it do or how does it work?

We designed AstroHealth as an offline-first clinical decision-support dashboard for astronauts and Crew Medical Officers (CMOs) across ISS (LEO), Lunar (Artemis), and Mars Transit (4–22 minute signal delays). Our platform monitors 18 physiological, behavioral, environmental, and operational indicators mapped across NASA’s 5 Human Research Program (HRP) Hazards and 6 anatomical health nodes.

Every check-in runs through our deterministic 4-stage JavaScript rules engine:

(1) absolute clinical cutoffs and 7 acute red-flag symptom overrides,

(2) z-score drift against each astronaut’s personal space-adapted baseline,

(3) 3-day monotonic worsening trend detection, and

(4) 0–100 composite scoring, A0/A1/A2 autonomy tracking, and measurement cadence alerts (DUE NOW / OVERDUE).

On screen, crews can explore alerts on our interactive 3D astronaut body map, view 7-day trend charts, log biometrics beside a live "? How" protocol drawer, run integrated PVT-Lite reaction tests and ONSD ultrasound caliper checks, follow an Earth-independent Mars triage checklist, export report packets, and optionally ask our AI protocol assistant.

What benefits does it have?

Zero-Connectivity Clinical Autonomy: Our system keeps clinical triage and step-by-step countermeasures working with zero connectivity or during 22-minute Mars communication blackouts.

Baseline-Aware Early Detection: By evaluating readings against each crew member’s space-adapted baseline, we reduce false alarms caused by normal microgravity physiology (such as slightly lower resting blood pressure), while our drift and trend stages catch silent deterioration early before a medical emergency develops. Additionally, our integrated "? How" procedure guides stay open side-by-side during check-ins to help crews prevent measurement errors.

Cognitive Load & Cabin Ergonomics: We deliberately engineered a low-glare dark theme and a single-screen, non-scrollable 3-column layout so fatigued crew members under time pressure see status, trends, and countermeasures simultaneously without scrolling or bright-screen fatigue.

Deterministic Safety vs. AI Hallucination Risk: All thresholds, alerts, and red-flag escalations live in a pure, deterministic JavaScript engine (src/engine/, verified by 33 Vitest tests), ensuring AI never invents medical diagnoses and strictly acts as a citable Q&A helper.

Citation Integrity & Unit Separation: Every indicator carries explicit [S], [L], [C], [H], HRP, and OSDR links to exact official sources, and our RadLab ingestion pipeline (scripts/radlab-daily.mjs) explicitly separates absorbed dose (µGy/day) in OSDR TEPC exports from dose equivalent (mSv/day) in NASA-STD-3001 limits.

Clear Prototype Scope: We transparently scoped and labeled AstroHealth as a clinical decision-support and hackathon prototype rather than a certified medical device.

What is the intended impact of the project?

Enabling Earth-Independent Deep Space Medicine: As humanity transitions from Low Earth Orbit (ISS) to sustained Artemis lunar operations and Mars transits with up to 22-minute communication delays, real-time ground telemedicine becomes impossible. We built AstroHealth to demonstrate how deterministic, evidence-linked clinical decision support can empower Crew Medical Officers (CMOs) to autonomously triage emergencies, track microgravity-adapted health baselines, and execute NASA-aligned countermeasures without relying on Earth Mission Control.

Bridging Terrestrial Extreme & Low-Resource Healthcare: Beyond spaceflight, our zero-connectivity browser architecture—bundling official clinical thresholds, side-by-side "? How" procedural guides, and self-contained diagnostics like PVT-Lite cognitive testing and ONSD ultrasound calipers—can be directly adapted for Earth's most isolated environments. This includes submarines, deep-sea maritime vessels, polar research stations, remote rural clinics, and disaster-response zones where internet infrastructure is unavailable and generalist responders need deterministic, hallucination-free clinical guidance.

What tools, coding languages, hardware, or software did you use to develop your project?

Frontend & 3D Visualization: We built AstroHealth using JavaScript (ES Modules), React 19, Vite, and Tailwind CSS v4, engineering a low-glare, non-scrollable 3-column dark interface. We used Three.js to render our interactive 3D EVA astronaut anatomical body map and Recharts for 7-day baseline drift trend visualizations.

Deterministic Clinical Engine & Testing: We decoupled our 4-stage clinical rules engine (src/engine/) from the UI and external APIs, validating all cutoffs, z-score drift calculations, and red-flag escalations with 33 automated tests in Vitest. For offline-first persistence across communication blackouts, we utilized browser localStorage alongside JSON/text report packet exports.

Data Ingestion & Clinical Reference Standards: We processed NASA OSDR RadLab ISS TEPC radiation telemetry (export.csv) via a custom Node.js aggregation pipeline (scripts/radlab-daily.mjs) that separates absorbed dose (µGy/day) from dose equivalent (mSv/day). We bundled evidence-linked reference thresholds and [S], [L], [C], and [H] citations directly from NASA-STD-3001 (Vol. 1 & Vol. 2), NASA HRP Risks & Hazards, NASA OCHMO Technical Briefs, and NIH MedlinePlus.

Deployment, AI & Hardware: We accelerated code generation and refactoring with GitHub Copilot and deployed the application on Vercel, using an optional /api/ask serverless function powered by the Google Gemini API as a strictly scoped, citable Q&A helper. No specialized external hardware is required—only a standard web browser.

How is your project creative?

Personalized Space-Adapted Baseline Modeling: Instead of applying generic Earth medical cutoffs in microgravity, we designed AstroHealth to calculate directional z-score drift around each astronaut’s space-adapted baseline alongside 3-day monotonic worsening trend detection—catching silent physiological deterioration early while eliminating false alarms from normal spaceflight adaptation.

Interactive 3D Anatomical Hazard Mapping: Rather than burying telemetry in static tables, we mapped NASA’s 5 Human Research Program (HRP) Hazards and 18 clinical indicators directly onto an interactive 3D EVA astronaut suit across 6 anatomical nodes, allowing crews to visually isolate affected organ systems at a glance.

Persistent "? How" Protocol Drawer & In-Browser Diagnostics: We paired every check-in input with a live, side-by-side "? How" procedure guide that stays open while logging vitals to prevent measurement errors under fatigue, and embedded interactive browser prototypes for ONSD ocular ultrasound caliper measurement and PVT-Lite reaction-time testing inside a zero-connectivity core.

Deterministic Triage with Hallucination-Free AI Guardrails: Instead of relying on generative AI for medical decisions, we engineered a pure, deterministic 4-stage JavaScript rules engine to govern all clinical cutoffs and red-flag escalations, restricting our optional Gemini AI assistant strictly to citable Q&A backed by NASA and MedlinePlus documentation.

What factors did your team consider?

Deep-Space Communication Blackouts & Offline Autonomy: With Mars transit signal delays reaching up to 22 minutes each way, real-time ground intervention is impossible. We decoupled our core JavaScript clinical engine from React and external APIs so every triage stage, trend chart, and checklist executes locally with zero internet connectivity.

Deterministic Safety vs. AI Hallucination Risk: In high-stakes clinical environments, probabilistic AI outputs cannot be trusted to make diagnostic calls. We isolated all medical thresholds, z-score drift math, and 7 acute red-flag escalations inside a pure, deterministic rules engine (verified by 33 automated Vitest tests), confining the optional Gemini API assistant strictly to citable Q&A.

Radiation Dosimetry Accuracy & Unit Separation: Space radiation telemetry uses distinct physical and biological metrics that cannot be conflated. Our Node.js ingestion pipeline (scripts/radlab-daily.mjs) explicitly separates absorbed dose (µGy/day) from NASA OSDR RadLab ISS TEPC exports from dose equivalent (mSv/day) in NASA-STD-3001 exposure limits.

Human Factors & Cabin Ergonomics: Fatigued astronauts operating under high cognitive load cannot afford screen glare or hunting across nested menus. We designed a low-glare dark interface with a single-screen, non-scrollable 3-column layout and a persistent "? How" protocol drawer so crews can view alerts, trends, and measurement guides simultaneously.

Evidence Traceability & Clinical Scope Boundaries: To ensure transparency and medical safety, we linked every indicator directly to official NASA-STD-3001, HRP, OCHMO, and NIH MedlinePlus sources ([S], [L], [C], [H] citations) while clearly scoping AstroHealth as an educational decision-support prototype rather than a certified medical device.
